Lets try it this way. If you are producing a new pen, then you need:

  • Ore

  • A workforce to extract raw materials

  • A workforce to convert raw materials

  • A workforce that assembles materials into a finished product

There are probably other steps involved, but lets keep this simple. Ore/Raw materials can be sourced from one business to another, but these would have to be sourced locally. If local materials are unavailable, then they can source it internationally. If all or some of these can be handled by local workers, then these must be done locally. If they can't, then said work can be outsourced to another country at the same rates/costs (or greater) of the business it resides in. In other words, if you were going to pay your local workers $25 per hour to assemble the product, then this is the amount you will pay to the workers you are outsourcing it to. If your hourly amount is below the countries minimum wage -- of where you're sourcing your workers from -- then you are obliged to pay more.

My point being, if it can be sourced locally, then it needs to done locally first at what ever the cheapest local rate is. Whether this would work short/long-term (if at all), I don't know. This is why I threw the idea out to see what everyone thinks.

This is a ridiculous question because production isn't "diverted" and jobs aren't "outsourced" in a way that can be measured controlled and regulated in a manner that would mean a law like could ever be enforceable.. The economy doesn't function in the static environment with classroom-simplistic examples like politicians and commentators like to depict in their pitches. You can't develop a political/idelogical preference and then try to analyze reality through that tinted lens, it just doesn't work out.

What If an old factory is shut down and a new one is opened ten miles awayr, was the production diverted?

What If the new factory is highly automated and requires half of the personnel was the work outsourced?

What if the old factory made printer paper and the new factory makes paper towels, but that company still has a printer paper factory in Canada that they import now?

What if the factory in Canada was operating at 40% capacity but now will operate at 85% capacity after old factory was shut down?

What if the old factory was expensive to run, would have been expensive to refit with modern tech, and was on a piece of prime real estate, and it made financial sense to redevelop the old factory into yuppie condos and build a new one that was designed around the modern tech from the group up?

Companies would collectively bitchslap whichever politicians had this bright idea until they folded or would have them taken out. The financial incentive is too large to ever be able to pull something like this off.

That being said, if it happened it would initially be chaos. So many companies rely on a globalized economy you would see a temporary economic depression as company after company went under and executives ran around like chickens with their heads removed. However, the need for localized infrastructure would probably make this depression short lasting. Overall it would strengthen some individual economies but lessen the net GDP of the entire world.
